newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan troops fight way into UNITA diamond areas.
newsitem.headline: Angolan troops fight way into UNITA diamond areas.

text.p: The Angolan army has pushed deeper into diamond-rich areas held by the UNITA opposition in the northeast and at least 65 soldiers have been wounded in clashes, a military source said on Thursday.
"We can confirm at least 65 FAA (Angolan Armed Forces) casualties, but those are only the ones we have seen. We have got no idea of the number of dead," the source said.
He added that fighting was continuing to the south of Nzage.

The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) said in a statement on Thursday it would airlift emergency food supplies for one month to Nzage to support about 3,000 people who have fled the hostilities.
It said this was in addition to supplementary food rations for 100 malnourished children in the town.
The WFP said on Wednesday over 2,000 people had arrived at Nzage because of the fighting, and a further 200 were arriving each day.

The Luanda government said its operation was intended to flush out armed refugees who had come across the border from the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, but analysts said this was a pretext to retake diamond-rich territory under the control of UNITA.

The government action has sparked new clashes between the two sides, who signed a peace treaty in 1994 to end a 20-year civil war. Analysts said the new tensions brought the treaty's long-term success into question in the diamond area.
Several foreign mining companies have suspended operations in Lunda Norte province because of the instability.
The military source said the army appeared to be reinforcing at the town of Cacolo, a government-held town in the Lunda Sul province, just south of where the fighting has been reported.
"It seems they may be preparing to try to take Xinge," the source said. Xinge is a strong UNITA-held town about 50 km (32 miles) northwest of Cacolo.
The source said it did not appear the government was planning strikes in other parts of the country, but feared retailiation by UNITA.

Since the signing of the peace pact the two sides have formed a unity government and begun integrating their armies, although over 50,000 UNITA troops are still in U.N. assembly camps awaiting demobilisation.

A UNITA official said on Thursday the movement had suspended the handover of territory under its control to the government. The state is meant to assume administrative control of the whole country under the 1994 treaty.
The process had ground to a halt, said Isaias Samakuva, UNITA's representative to the body overseeing the peace process. "There are just too many problems at the moment,'' he said.
"We have decided to suspend the process for a time while we talk with Bailundo about what to do next," he said, referring to the central highlands city where UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi is based.
There was no immediate response from the government.
Some estimates put the area under UNITA control at up to 70 percent of the countryside, including the diamond areas which provide the movement with up to $600 million annually.
The fall of Mobutu Sese Seko's government in former Zaire in May was a major blow to UNITA, which had used the country as its weapons and supplies base.
The organisation began allowing the state to reestablish administrations in some places after April 30, the process starting with the handover of M'Banza Congo in the northwest.
But UNITA supporters have ripped down state flags there several times, as they have in cities in the central highlands.
Samakuva and several government officials were badly beaten by UNITA supporters at a handover ceremony in Quibala, about 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Luanda, on May 30.
"People in Angola have been separated for a very long time," said Samakuva. "They do not understand this change that is taking place, and many of them do not like it."
